newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand was frail at the close, but off its worst levels, after a hectic day of trade which saw it sink to a fresh all-time low against the dollar and the British pound.
Key long bonds weakened to their worst levels in two months, succumbing to a steady bout of selling and profit-taking which accompanied the rand's slide.
Dealers said late trading on the currency market consisted of players squaring positions ahead of the weekend, with the market weary after the earlier frenetic activity.
"Guys are trying to square up their positions, taking any profits," said one dealer.
"The (dollar) buyers also look to be out of the market."

The rand ended at 4.6110/6160 on the U.S dollar from 4.5840/90 Thursday close. Earlier in the afternoon the local unit dived to a worst level of 4.6150 bid, a move blamed on dollar buying out of London.
In after-hours the unit slid even further to a worst ever 4.62 bid.
"The London investment house that was in the market yesterday (Thursday) was again taking dollars," a dealer said.
The size of the order was believed to be in the region of $200 to $300 million dollars, traders said.
"When the rand pushed through the 4.60 level (on the upside), there was panic and stop losses were triggered," another dealer said.
Dealers said some profit-taking was seen around the 4.61-4.6125 level which capped the slide for a while.
The central Reserve Bank was also evident at the market's top levels for most of the afternoon, providing liquidity.
Against the crosses, the rand fell to a new low of 7.3862 bid against the British pound from 7.2888/2991 late on Thursday. On the mark, the rand was at 0.3295/3300 from 0.3320/3325 previously.
On the bond market yields were near the day's worst levels in late trading with the key R150 at 15.73 percent from 15.635 percent overnight.

The R150 touched the day's worst level of 15.76 percent on a combination of rand weakness, comments from Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals and a softer U.S. Treasury market following September durable goods orders which pointed to a possible U.S. interest rate hike.
"When the rand got through the key 4.60 level a lot of people turned sellers (of bonds)," a dealer said.

Yields ticked higher after Stals said the central bank may need to tighten monetary policy. His assurance shortly thereafter that there was no immediate need to hike interest rates helped rates off their worst.
Dealers said late trade on Friday was characterised by profit-taking ahead of the weekend.
They said the market was seen strengthening on Monday to around the 15.67 percent level if money supply data came in as expected.

Economists forecast M3 would grow at a slower rate of 15.1 percent in September compared with a preliminary 15.51 percent in August. Private sector credit extension was expected to ease to 17.3 from 17.71 percent in August.
Bond Exchange figures show foreigners bought a net 48.79 million rand worth of South African bonds on Thursday after buying 244.71 million rand the previous day.
Nominal cumulative volumes were pegged at 38.24 billion rand on Thursday -- a settlement day -- from 3.76 billion rand on Wednesday.
On the money market, three-month NCDs were steady at between 16.15 percent bid and 16 percent. The 90-day BA rate was unchanged at between 15.55 and 15.40 percent.
The Reserve Bank indicated the daily shortage slightly lower at 7.638 billion from 7.887 billion rand on Thursday.
-- Nicole Mordant, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
